overview: On-call for data teams means a named engineer is responsible, around the clock or during agreed hours, for responding to alerts about broken, late, or wrong data, not just infrastructure being down.

Unlike classic web SRE where a page usually means a service is unavailable, data on-call fires on pipeline failures (an Airflow DAG failing), freshness breaches (a Snowflake table not updated by SLA), and quality violations (a dbt test or Great Expectations check failing).

A runbook is the pre-written, step-by-step response guide attached to an alert that turns a stressful 3 AM page into a mechanical procedure: what broke, who it affects, how to diagnose it, how to mitigate it, and when to escalate.
learningObjectives: Explain what on-call means specifically for data engineering teams and how it differs from generic infrastructure SRE.
Describe primary/secondary rotations, escalation policies, and alert severity levels (P1-P4, actionable vs FYI).
Write a good runbook containing symptom, impact, diagnosis, mitigation, escalation, and links to dashboards and lineage.
Define and interpret MTTA and MTTR and use on-call health metrics to reduce alert fatigue and pager noise.
Identify opportunities for self-healing and auto-remediation of common data failures such as retries and backfills.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: On-call is an operational practice in which a designated engineer (and one or more escalation tiers) is accountable for acknowledging and resolving production incidents within defined time targets, governed by a rotation schedule, an escalation policy, and severity-based alerting; runbooks are the versioned, per-alert operational documents that codify the diagnosis and remediation procedure so incidents can be handled consistently and quickly regardless of who is paged.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Think of on-call as being the emergency doctor on duty for your data pipelines. When something breaks in the middle of the night, the pager goes off and you are the one who responds. A runbook is the emergency handbook next to the phone: it tells you what the symptom means, who is affected, the exact checks to run, how to stop the bleeding, and who to call if you are stuck. Good on-call is not about heroics; it is about having clear rotations, sensible alerts, and runbooks so any engineer can fix the problem calmly.
coreConcept.historicalContext: On-call rotations originated in traditional IT operations and telecom, then were formalized by Google's SRE practice in the 2000s with concepts like error budgets, toil reduction, and blameless postmortems (popularized by the 2016 SRE book). PagerDuty (founded 2009) and later Opsgenie made escalation policies and rotations mainstream. Data engineering inherited these practices later: as pipelines became business-critical and the modern data stack (Airflow ~2015, dbt ~2016, the data observability wave ~2019 with Monte Carlo) matured, teams realized that a green DAG is not the same as correct, fresh data, and adapted on-call to page on freshness, volume, and quality SLAs, not only crashes.

whyItMatters.business: Stale or wrong data feeds executive dashboards, financial reports, billing, and ML features; a fast, well-run on-call function limits data downtime, protects revenue and regulatory compliance, and preserves stakeholder trust in the data platform.
whyItMatters.engineering: Runbooks and clear rotations convert tribal knowledge into repeatable procedures, so incidents are resolved by whoever is on-call rather than by hunting down the one person who understands a fragile pipeline.
whyItMatters.scalability: As the number of DAGs, dbt models, and Kafka topics grows into the thousands, ad-hoc firefighting does not scale; severity-tiered alerting, ownership, and auto-remediation are the only way to keep operational load flat as the platform grows.
whyItMatters.cost: Every hour of data downtime has a cost in wrong decisions and reprocessing compute; reducing MTTR and auto-remediating common failures (transient retries, automatic backfills) cuts both incident cost and engineer burnout.
whyItMatters.reliability: Defined SLAs, escalation policies, and on-call health metrics make the reliability of data products measurable and enforceable, the same way uptime SLOs do for services.

coreComponents.name: Rotation Schedule
coreComponents.definition: A calendar assigning who is the primary and secondary on-call responder for each time window, typically weekly for data teams.
coreComponents.purpose: To guarantee that at any moment there is a clearly identified, single owner responsible for responding to pages, with a backup.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Rotate fairly across the team, define primary and secondary tiers, support overrides for holidays or illness, and enable follow-the-sun handoffs across regions.
coreComponents.examples: A weekly PagerDuty schedule where the primary is paged first and the secondary is paged if the primary does not acknowledge within 10 minutes; a follow-the-sun setup where EMEA holds the pager during their day and hands to US-West at end of shift.

coreComponents.name: Escalation Policy
coreComponents.definition: The rules that determine who gets notified, in what order, and after how long if an alert is not acknowledged or resolved.
coreComponents.purpose: To ensure an unanswered or unresolved incident reliably reaches someone with more context or authority instead of being silently dropped.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Define acknowledgement timeouts, cascade from primary to secondary to team lead to engineering manager, and specify when to loop in adjacent teams (platform, upstream data producers).
coreComponents.examples: Primary paged immediately; if no ack in 10 minutes escalate to secondary; if still unacked in 20 minutes page the data platform lead; a P1 also notifies the incident channel and the on-call manager.

coreComponents.name: Alert Severity Levels
coreComponents.definition: A classification (commonly P1-P4) of how urgent and impactful an alert is, distinguishing actionable pages from FYI notifications.
coreComponents.purpose: To route the right response urgency to the right channel so critical issues page a human immediately while low-priority signals go to a queue or dashboard.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Map each alert to a severity, define response-time expectations per level, and keep P1/P2 reserved for genuinely actionable, business-impacting events.
coreComponents.examples: P1: revenue dashboard source table missing before market open, pages immediately 24/7. P4: a non-critical dev table freshness warning, posted to a Slack channel with no page.

coreComponents.name: Runbook
coreComponents.definition: A versioned document attached to an alert that describes the symptom, impact, diagnosis steps, mitigation, escalation path, and links to dashboards and lineage.
coreComponents.purpose: To let any on-call engineer diagnose and resolve a specific failure quickly and consistently without needing the original author's memory.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Stay current with the pipeline, provide copy-pasteable diagnosis commands, describe safe mitigations (retry, backfill, rollback), and state clear escalation criteria.
coreComponents.examples: A runbook for 'orders_daily DAG failed' with exact Airflow CLI commands to inspect the failed task, a dbt command to re-run the failing model, and a link to the OpenLineage graph and the Grafana freshness dashboard.

coreComponents.name: Incident Response Workflow
coreComponents.definition: The end-to-end process from alert firing to acknowledgement, mitigation, resolution, and postmortem.
coreComponents.purpose: To give a repeatable structure to handling incidents so nothing is missed under pressure and learning is captured afterward.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Track MTTA and MTTR, coordinate communication with stakeholders during outages, and drive blameless postmortems for significant incidents.
coreComponents.examples: PagerDuty alert -> engineer acknowledges (MTTA clock stops) -> runs runbook diagnosis -> re-runs backfill (mitigation) -> confirms freshness restored (MTTR clock stops) -> writes postmortem for the P1.

internalWorking: A monitoring source (Prometheus, an Airflow on_failure_callback, a dbt test result, a freshness check on Snowflake, or a Great Expectations checkpoint) emits a signal when a condition is violated.
That signal is sent to an alerting platform such as PagerDuty or Opsgenie with a severity, a summary, a dedup key, and a link to the corresponding runbook.
The alerting platform consults the current rotation schedule to find the primary on-call engineer and notifies them via push, SMS, or phone according to the severity and their notification rules.
If the primary does not acknowledge within the configured timeout, the escalation policy cascades the page to the secondary, then to leads, ensuring the incident is not dropped.
The engineer acknowledges (stopping the MTTA clock), opens the linked runbook, follows the diagnosis and mitigation steps, and resolves the alert (stopping the MTTR clock).
Metrics such as MTTA, MTTR, page volume, and after-hours pages are recorded so the team can measure on-call health, tune noisy alerts, and identify candidates for auto-remediation.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Signal source (Airflow callback / dbt test / freshness check / Prometheus rule) -> Alert with severity + dedup key + runbook link -> PagerDuty/Opsgenie -> Rotation schedule resolves primary -> Notify (push/SMS/call) -> Ack (MTTA stops) or escalate to secondary/lead -> Open runbook -> Diagnose -> Mitigate (retry/backfill/rollback) -> Resolve (MTTR stops) -> Postmortem + metrics feedback
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. At 05:40 an Airflow on_failure_callback fires because the orders_daily DAG's dbt_run task failed, sending a P2 event to PagerDuty with a dedup key and a link to the orders runbook.
2. PagerDuty looks up the weekly rotation, finds the primary on-call engineer, and pushes a notification to their phone.
3. The engineer acknowledges within 4 minutes (MTTA = 4 min) and opens the linked runbook, which points to the failing dbt model and the freshness dashboard.
4. Following the diagnosis steps, they find the upstream stg_orders table had a null spike that broke a not_null test, quarantine the bad rows, and re-run the model with a targeted dbt build.

5. Freshness is restored by 06:15, the alert auto-resolves when the freshness check passes, MTTR is recorded as 35 minutes, and because this failure mode is recurring the team files a task to add an automatic quarantine-and-retry step.

keyTerminology.meaning: Being the designated responder accountable for production incidents during a defined window.
keyTerminology.importance: It guarantees a single clear owner for incidents so data outages are addressed promptly rather than falling through the cracks.

keyTerminology.meaning: A per-alert document with symptom, impact, diagnosis, mitigation, escalation, and links.
keyTerminology.importance: It lets any engineer resolve an incident consistently without depending on one person's memory.

keyTerminology.meaning: The ordered rules for who is notified and when if an alert is not acknowledged or resolved.
keyTerminology.importance: It ensures unanswered incidents reliably reach someone with more context instead of being dropped.

keyTerminology.meaning: Mean Time To Acknowledge: the average time from an alert firing to a human acknowledging it.
keyTerminology.importance: It measures how fast the team responds and exposes rotation or notification problems.

keyTerminology.meaning: Mean Time To Resolve (or Recover): the average time from alert to full resolution.
keyTerminology.importance: It quantifies data downtime and is the primary target for runbooks and auto-remediation.

keyTerminology.meaning: Desensitization caused by too many, especially non-actionable, alerts.
keyTerminology.importance: Fatigued engineers miss real P1s, so reducing pager noise is essential to reliability.

keyTerminology.meaning: A commitment that a table or dataset will be updated by a specific time, e.g. by 06:00.
keyTerminology.importance: Freshness breaches are a primary data on-call trigger even when jobs technically succeed.

keyTerminology.meaning: Rotating on-call ownership across geographic regions so someone is always on duty during daytime hours.
keyTerminology.importance: It reduces night pages and burnout for globally distributed data teams.

importantConcepts.concept: Paging on data, not just infrastructure
importantConcepts.explanation: What: data on-call fires on freshness, volume, and quality violations, not only crashes. Why: a DAG can succeed while loading stale or wrong data. How: wire alerts from dbt tests, freshness checks, and observability tools into the pager, not just from server health. Pitfall: teams that only page on infrastructure discover data incidents only when a stakeholder complains hours later.

importantConcepts.concept: Every actionable alert needs a runbook
importantConcepts.explanation: What: an alert that pages a human must link to a document telling them what to do. Why: pages arrive at 3 AM to whoever is on-call, not the author. How: make a runbook link a required field for any P1/P2 alert and store runbooks in version control next to pipeline code. Pitfall: naked alerts with no runbook cause long MTTR and force escalation for issues that should be self-serve.

What: only alerts that require immediate human action should page; everything else is a notification. Why: paging on FYI events causes alert fatigue and missed real incidents. How: reserve P1/P2 for business-impacting, actionable events and route P3/P4 to Slack, tickets, or dashboards. Pitfall: labeling everything urgent trains the team to ignore the pager.

What: common, well-understood failures (transient network errors, a late upstream partition) can be fixed by code before a human is paged. Why: it reduces toil and MTTR and protects sleep. How: use Airflow task retries with backoff, automatic backfills for late partitions, and idempotent loads so retries are safe. Pitfall: auto-retrying a non-transient failure (bad schema) just delays the real fix and hides the signal.

variationsAndTypes: **Primary vs secondary rotation:** the primary responds first; the secondary is the backup if the primary is unreachable or overwhelmed.
**Follow-the-sun rotation:** ownership passes between regions so on-call happens during local daytime and night pages are minimized.
**Business-hours vs 24/7 on-call:** critical, always-on data products need 24/7 coverage while lower-tier pipelines may only be covered during working hours.
**Team-based vs platform-based on-call:** domain teams own their own pipelines, or a central data platform team owns shared infrastructure like Airflow and Kafka.
**Actionable pages vs FYI notifications:** high-severity actionable alerts page a human, while informational signals go to a channel or ticket queue.
**Manual runbooks vs automated runbooks:** human-followed markdown/YAML runbooks versus codified auto-remediation that executes steps automatically.
advantages: **Fast, consistent incident response:** a clear owner plus a runbook means issues are resolved quickly regardless of who is paged.
**Reduced data downtime:** freshness and quality alerts catch problems in minutes instead of hours, shrinking MTTR.
**Knowledge sharing:** runbooks turn tribal knowledge into documented, repeatable procedures the whole team can use.
**Measurable reliability:** MTTA, MTTR, and page volume make on-call health and data-product reliability quantifiable.
**Lower burnout when done well:** sensible severity tiers, follow-the-sun, and auto-remediation reduce night pages and toil.
disadvantages: **Burnout risk:** poorly tuned alerting and unfair rotations cause fatigue, missed pages, and attrition.
**Maintenance overhead:** runbooks and alert thresholds must be kept current or they become misleading and untrusted.
**Alert fatigue:** too many non-actionable pages desensitize engineers so they miss genuine P1s.
**Coverage gaps:** small teams struggle to staff 24/7 rotations without excessive individual load.
**False confidence:** having runbooks does not help if they are stale, incomplete, or not linked to the alert.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Establish formal on-call with runbooks for business-critical data products with SLAs (revenue, billing, regulatory, customer-facing metrics, production ML features) and for shared platform components like Airflow, Kafka, and the warehouse.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid heavyweight 24/7 paging and detailed runbooks for transient dev tables, exploratory pipelines, or low-stakes internal datasets where a business-hours ticket or dashboard warning is sufficient and full on-call cost is not justified.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Data on-call is like a hospital emergency department. Doctors work in shifts so someone is always on duty (the rotation), and there is a clear order for who gets called in when a case is beyond the first responder (the escalation policy). Cases are triaged by urgency, so a heart attack is seen immediately while a sprained ankle waits (severity levels). Each condition has a treatment protocol pinned to the wall so any doctor on shift knows the steps (the runbook). Hospitals track how fast patients are seen and treated (MTTA and MTTR), and routine cases follow standing orders that nurses can act on without waking a specialist (auto-remediation).

commonMisconceptions.myth: On-call for data teams is the same as web SRE, so a page always means something is down.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Data on-call frequently pages on freshness, volume, and quality violations while all the servers are healthy and the jobs report success; a DAG can be green while the data is stale or wrong.
Too many alerts, especially non-actionable ones, cause alert fatigue that makes engineers miss the real P1s; fewer, well-tuned, actionable alerts with runbooks give better real coverage.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A runbook is optional documentation you write later.
commonMisconceptions.reality: For any alert that pages a human, the runbook is part of the alert itself; without it, on-call resolution is slow and depends on the original author's memory.

productionConsiderations.scalability: As DAGs, dbt models, and topics scale into the thousands, tier alerts by data value, group related alerts to avoid storms, and codify auto-remediation so operational load stays flat rather than growing linearly with pipeline count.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Make alerts deduplicated and self-resolving (auto-resolve when the freshness check passes), keep runbooks in version control next to pipeline code, and test escalation policies so an unacked page always reaches a human.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Design idempotent loads (MERGE, delete-insert by partition) so retries and backfills are safe, use Airflow retries with exponential backoff for transient failures, and quarantine bad rows rather than failing whole batches.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Track on-call health metrics (MTTA, MTTR, total pages, after-hours pages, percent auto-resolved) on a dashboard and review them regularly to tune noisy alerts and spot burnout.
productionConsiderations.security: Restrict who can silence or resolve pages, avoid putting sensitive data values in alert payloads and runbook logs, and use least-privilege service accounts for auto-remediation actions like backfills.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Auto-remediate transient failures before paging to cut toil, prune always-firing or always-passing alerts, and reserve expensive full-table reconciliation checks for critical tables on a cadence.
productionConsiderations.performance: Keep runbook diagnosis commands fast and copy-pasteable, use partition-scoped backfills instead of full reprocessing, and ensure alerting latency is low so MTTA is not inflated by slow notification delivery.

codeExamples.title: Airflow on_failure_callback that pages PagerDuty
codeExamples.overview: An Airflow callback that fires when a task fails, builds a severity-tagged PagerDuty Events API v2 payload with a dedup key and a runbook link, so the on-call engineer is paged with context.
codeExamples.code:
import os
import requests

PD_EVENTS_URL = "https://events.pagerduty.com/v2/enqueue"
RUNBOOK_BASE = "https://runbooks.internal/dag"

def page_pagerduty(context):
    ti = context["task_instance"]
    dag_id = ti.dag_id
    task_id = ti.task_id
    run_id = context["run_id"]
    log_url = ti.log_url

    # P1 for revenue-critical DAGs, else P2
    severity = "critical" if dag_id.startswith("revenue_") else "error"

    payload = {
        "routing_key": os.environ["PAGERDUTY_ROUTING_KEY"],
        "event_action": "trigger",
        # dedup_key groups repeated failures of the same task into one incident
        "dedup_key": f"{dag_id}.{task_id}",
        "payload": {
            "summary": f"[{severity.upper()}] {dag_id}.{task_id} failed ({run_id})",
            "source": "airflow",
            "severity": severity,
            "custom_details": {
                "runbook": f"{RUNBOOK_BASE}/{dag_id}.md",
                "log_url": log_url,
                "run_id": run_id,
            },
        },
        "links": [{"href": f"{RUNBOOK_BASE}/{dag_id}.md", "text": "Runbook"}],
    }
    resp = requests.post(PD_EVENTS_URL, json=payload, timeout=10)
    resp.raise_for_status()

# Wire it into the DAG default_args so every task uses it
default_args = {
    "retries": 2,
    "retry_delay": __import__("datetime").timedelta(minutes=5),
    "on_failure_callback": page_pagerduty,
}
codeExamples.breakdown: The callback receives Airflow's context, extracts the failing task and its log URL, and derives severity from the DAG name so revenue DAGs page as critical (P1). The dedup_key ensures repeated failures of the same task collapse into one incident instead of a page storm. The custom_details and links carry the runbook URL and log directly into the page, and default_args first applies two retries with a 5-minute delay so transient failures self-heal before anyone is paged.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: On a task failure, PagerDuty returns HTTP 202 with a dedup_key, and the on-call engineer receives a push/SMS titled '[ERROR] orders_daily.dbt_run failed (scheduled__2026-07-03)' containing a clickable runbook link and the Airflow log URL.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Paging on the first attempt instead of after retries (noisy); no dedup_key so every retry creates a new incident; hardcoding the routing key in code; the callback itself throwing and masking the original task error.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Only page after retries are exhausted by relying on default_args retries, set dedup_key per task, keep severity mapping in a config table not code, and wrap the requests call in a try/except so a paging failure never hides the underlying task failure.

codeExamples.title: Runbook Template (YAML) for a Pipeline Alert
codeExamples.overview: A structured, version-controlled runbook template capturing the anatomy of a good runbook: symptom, impact, severity, diagnosis steps, mitigation, escalation, and links to dashboards and lineage.
codeExamples.code:
# runbooks/orders_daily.yaml
alert: orders_daily.dbt_run failed
owner: analytics-eng@company.com
severity: P2            # P1 24/7 page, P2 page, P3 ticket, P4 FYI
slo:
  freshness: "orders table updated by 06:00 UTC"

symptom: >
  The orders_daily DAG's dbt_run task failed, or the orders table
  freshness check has not passed by 06:00 UTC.

impact: >
  Executive revenue dashboard and finance daily report show stale
  numbers. Approx. 40 downstream dbt models depend on this table.

diagnosis:
  - "Check the failed task log linked in the PagerDuty alert."
  - "airflow tasks states-for-dag-run orders_daily <run_id>"
  - "Inspect the dbt test that failed: dbt test --select stg_orders"
  - "Check upstream freshness: is the raw.orders source late?"
  - "Confirm blast radius in lineage (link below) before re-running."

mitigation:
  - "Transient error: re-run the single task -> airflow tasks run orders_daily dbt_run <run_id>"
  - "Null spike broke not_null test: quarantine bad rows, then dbt build --select stg_orders+"
  - "Upstream late: wait for raw.orders, then trigger backfill for the partition (see below)."

backfill: "airflow dags backfill orders_daily -s 2026-07-03 -e 2026-07-03 --reset-dagruns"

escalation:
  - "No resolution in 30 min or upstream source broken -> page ingestion-team secondary."
  - "If P1 (before market open) -> notify #data-incidents and on-call manager."

links:
  dashboard: "https://grafana.internal/d/orders-freshness"
  lineage: "https://lineage.internal/openlineage/orders"
  dbt_docs: "https://dbt-docs.internal/#!/model/model.orders"
codeExamples.breakdown: The header ties the alert to an owner, a severity level, and the concrete freshness SLO it protects. Symptom tells the responder what they are seeing; impact quantifies blast radius (dashboards plus ~40 downstream models) so they can judge urgency. Diagnosis is an ordered list of copy-pasteable Airflow and dbt commands; mitigation maps each likely root cause to a specific safe action including the backfill command; escalation states exactly when and whom to page next; links point straight to the freshness dashboard, OpenLineage graph, and dbt docs.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: A rendered runbook page the on-call engineer opens from the alert, letting them go from page to resolution by following ordered steps, e.g. run the diagnosis commands, identify a null spike, quarantine, and run 'dbt build --select stg_orders+' to restore freshness.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Runbooks that describe theory instead of exact commands; missing lineage/dashboard links so blast radius is unknown; stale commands after the pipeline changed; no clear escalation trigger.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Store runbooks in the same repo as the pipeline so they version together, lint that every P1/P2 alert has a runbook link in CI, and include the exact idempotent backfill command so re-runs are safe.

codeExamples.title: Triage: diagnose a failed dbt run and re-run a backfill
codeExamples.overview: A bash triage snippet an on-call engineer runs to inspect a failed Airflow DAG run and dbt failure, then safely re-run the affected models and a partition backfill.
codeExamples.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
DAG=orders_daily
RUN_ID="${1:?usage: triage.sh <run_id> <ds>}"
DS="${2:?usage: triage.sh <run_id> <ds>}"

echo "== Task states for $DAG $RUN_ID =="
airflow tasks states-for-dag-run "$DAG" "$RUN_ID"

echo "== Which dbt test/model failed =="
# dbt writes machine-readable results here after each run
jq -r '.results[] | select(.status=="fail" or .status=="error")
        | "\(.status)\t\(.unique_id)"' target/run_results.json || true

echo "== Freshness of the source in Snowflake =="
snowsql -q "SELECT MAX(event_timestamp) AS latest,
  DATEDIFF('minute', MAX(event_timestamp), CURRENT_TIMESTAMP) AS lag_min
  FROM raw.orders;"

# If root cause is a transient/model error, rebuild the model and its children
echo "== Re-running failed model and downstream =="
dbt build --select stg_orders+ --target prod

# If a partition was missed, run an idempotent backfill for that day only
echo "== Backfilling partition $DS =="
airflow dags backfill "$DAG" -s "$DS" -e "$DS" --reset-dagruns --yes

echo "== Confirm freshness restored =="
snowsql -q "SELECT DATEDIFF('minute', MAX(event_timestamp), CURRENT_TIMESTAMP) AS lag_min FROM analytics.orders;"
codeExamples.breakdown: It first lists task states to see exactly which Airflow task failed, then parses dbt's run_results.json with jq to name the failing model or test. It checks source freshness in Snowflake to decide whether the root cause is upstream lateness or a code/data error. 'dbt build --select stg_orders+' rebuilds the failing model and everything downstream of it; the partition-scoped backfill with --reset-dagruns is idempotent so it only reprocesses the affected day; the final query confirms the freshness lag is back within SLA.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Console output showing failed task states, a line like 'fail\tmodel.analytics.stg_orders', a source lag of e.g. 8 minutes, successful dbt and backfill runs, and a final lag_min under the SLA threshold confirming recovery.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Backfilling a wide date range and reprocessing far more than needed; non-idempotent loads that duplicate rows on re-run; running dbt build without '+' and leaving stale downstream models; assuming the failure is transient without checking source freshness.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Always scope backfills to the affected partition, ensure loads are idempotent (MERGE/delete-insert) before re-running, use dbt's '+' selector to refresh downstream models, and end every triage by verifying the freshness SLA rather than assuming success.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A fintech's daily orders table feeds the executive revenue dashboard (needed by 06:30 UTC before market open), the finance close report, and a fraud ML feature. Previously, when the orders pipeline broke overnight, nobody noticed until an executive complained at 09:00, causing hours of data downtime and lost trust. The goal is a data on-call setup with runbooks so freshness and quality failures page the right engineer and are resolved before stakeholders are affected.
endToEndExample.inputData: Raw order events streamed via Kafka into a raw.orders landing table in Snowflake, transformed by dbt into stg_orders and analytics.orders, orchestrated by an Airflow DAG orders_daily that runs at 05:00 UTC.
endToEndExample.architecture: Kafka -> raw.orders (Snowflake) -> Airflow DAG orders_daily runs dbt build -> stg_orders and analytics.orders. An Airflow on_failure_callback and a scheduled freshness check both feed PagerDuty with severity and a runbook link. A weekly primary/secondary rotation and an escalation policy route pages; Prometheus/Grafana track freshness and on-call metrics; OpenLineage provides the dependency graph.
processingSteps: 1. The freshness SLO is defined: analytics.orders must be updated by 06:00 UTC, checked every 15 minutes; the DAG has 2 retries with 5-minute backoff so transient errors self-heal.
2. On any task failure after retries, the on_failure_callback pages PagerDuty with a dedup key, severity (P1 for revenue DAGs), and the orders_daily runbook link.
3. PagerDuty resolves the current primary from the weekly rotation and notifies them; if unacked in 10 minutes it escalates to the secondary, then the platform lead.
4. The on-call engineer acknowledges, opens the runbook, runs the diagnosis commands (task states, dbt run_results, source freshness), and checks blast radius in OpenLineage.

5. Root cause is a null spike in raw.orders that broke a not_null test; the engineer quarantines the bad rows, re-runs 'dbt build --select stg_orders+', and confirms freshness is restored, auto-resolving the alert.
endToEndExample.output: A fresh, validated analytics.orders table by 06:12 UTC, well before the 06:30 dashboard deadline; a resolved PagerDuty incident with recorded MTTA and MTTR; and a follow-up ticket to auto-quarantine null spikes so this failure mode self-heals next time.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Grafana dashboards show orders freshness lag against the 06:00 SLA and on-call health metrics (MTTA, MTTR, weekly page count, after-hours pages, percent auto-resolved). PagerDuty analytics show escalation rates and per-alert noise.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Transient failures are absorbed by Airflow retries before paging. Quality failures quarantine bad rows rather than failing the whole batch. Upstream lateness triggers a partition-scoped backfill. If the root cause is an upstream Kafka/ingestion problem, the runbook escalates to the ingestion team's secondary on-call.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Data downtime for the orders pipeline dropped from hours to minutes: incidents now page the on-call engineer directly with a runbook, MTTA fell to under 5 minutes and MTTR to about 30 minutes, executives receive fresh dashboards on time, and recurring failure modes are progressively auto-remediated, reducing night pages and burnout.

industryUseCases.problem: A massive number of data pipelines feeding personalization and analytics meant on-call engineers were overwhelmed by failures and manual reruns, creating heavy operational toil.
industryUseCases.solution: Netflix invested in data pipeline auto-remediation and self-healing (for example their Pensive/auto-recovery style tooling) that classifies failures and automatically retries or reruns transient ones before a human is paged.
industryUseCases.benefits: A large share of pipeline failures self-heal without paging anyone, drastically reducing on-call toil and MTTR while letting engineers focus on genuine, novel incidents.

industryUseCases.problem: Data teams learned about freshness, volume, and schema incidents only after stakeholders complained, with no clear owner or runbook to respond.
industryUseCases.solution: A data observability platform that detects freshness/volume/schema/distribution anomalies, routes them to the right owner via PagerDuty/Opsgenie/Slack with lineage-based blast-radius context.
industryUseCases.benefits: Data incidents page the correct on-call owner with root-cause and impact context, cutting time-to-detection and MTTR and reducing data downtime.

industryUseCases.problem: With thousands of pipelines and models, on-call engineers needed to understand ownership and downstream impact fast to respond to data incidents effectively.
industryUseCases.solution: Airbnb built internal data tooling (data portal, lineage, and dataset certification) that surfaces ownership and dependencies, which on-call responders use to assess blast radius during incidents.
industryUseCases.benefits: On-call engineers can immediately see who owns a dataset and what depends on it, speeding triage, escalation, and communication during data incidents.

industryUseCases.problem: Business-critical data pipelines needed reliable, on-time delivery, and ad-hoc firefighting did not scale as the data platform grew.
industryUseCases.solution: Formal data on-call with severity-tiered alerting on freshness and quality SLAs, runbooks stored with pipeline code, and escalation policies in Opsgenie/PagerDuty.
industryUseCases.benefits: Consistent, fast incident response with measurable MTTA/MTTR and reduced data downtime for revenue-critical datasets, plus lower reliance on individual heroics.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Tier alerts and runbooks by data value so the thousands of pipelines do not all page 24/7; group related alerts with dedup keys to prevent page storms; and push routine recovery into auto-remediation so operational load stays flat as pipeline count grows.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Use Airflow task retries with exponential backoff for transient errors, idempotent loads (MERGE or delete-insert by partition) so backfills and reruns cannot duplicate data, and quarantine bad rows rather than failing entire batches.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Run alerting and rotations on managed platforms (PagerDuty/Opsgenie) with multi-channel notification (push, SMS, phone) so a single failed channel does not drop a page, and always define a secondary and escalation tier.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Keep runbooks version-controlled with the pipeline so recovery procedures survive outages, store idempotent backfill commands so any window can be reprocessed, and retain source data (Kafka retention, raw landing tables) long enough to rebuild derived tables after an incident.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Keep runbook diagnosis commands fast and copy-pasteable, scope backfills to affected partitions instead of full reprocessing, and minimize alerting latency so MTTA reflects human response, not notification lag.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Auto-remediate transient failures before paging to cut human toil, prune noisy always-firing or always-passing alerts, and reserve expensive full-table reconciliation for critical tables on a cadence rather than every run.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Restrict who can silence/resolve incidents and who can run auto-remediation actions like backfills (least-privilege service accounts), and avoid including sensitive data values in alert payloads, runbooks, and logs.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Track freshness, volume, and schema alongside on-call health metrics (MTTA, MTTR, page volume, after-hours pages, percent auto-resolved) in Grafana and PagerDuty analytics, and review them in regular operational reviews.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Wire dbt tests and Great Expectations checkpoints into the pager so quality violations (null spikes, failed uniqueness, distribution shifts) trigger incidents with severity, not just silent test failures buried in logs.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Attach a dedup key, severity, runbook link, and log URL to every alert; make alerts self-resolve when the underlying check passes; route P1/P2 to the pager and P3/P4 to Slack or tickets to control noise.

recommendedPractices: **Attach a runbook to every actionable alert**, and make the runbook link a required field for any P1/P2 page.
**Reserve paging for actionable, business-impacting events**; route FYI signals to Slack, tickets, or dashboards to prevent alert fatigue.
**Define primary and secondary rotations plus an escalation policy** so no unacknowledged incident is ever dropped.
**Auto-remediate known transient failures** with retries, idempotent backfills, and quarantine before paging a human.
**Do a structured handoff** at the end of each rotation covering open incidents, known-flaky pipelines, and in-flight backfills.
engineeringStandards: Runbooks live in version control next to the pipeline code and are updated in the same PR when the pipeline changes.
Every business-critical dataset has a named owner, a freshness/quality SLA, and an escalation path.
Alerts carry a severity, a dedup key, and a runbook link, and self-resolve when the underlying check passes.
designRecommendations: Tier alert severity and runbook rigor by data value so critical products get 24/7 paging and low-stakes tables get tickets.
Make all loads idempotent so retries and backfills are always safe to re-run.
Prefer follow-the-sun or business-hours coverage where possible to minimize night pages and burnout.
namingConventions: Name alerts by pipeline, object, and condition, for example orders_daily__freshness__stale or stg_orders__not_null__failed.
Name runbook files after the alert or DAG, for example runbooks/orders_daily.yaml, so the link is predictable.
Name severity levels consistently (P1-P4) with a documented meaning and response-time expectation for each.
documentationStandards: Document each runbook with the same sections: symptom, impact, severity, diagnosis, mitigation, escalation, and links.
Document the escalation policy and rotation schedule so everyone knows who responds and when it cascades.
Document on-call expectations and a handoff checklist so responders know their responsibilities each shift.
testingStrategies: Run game days / fire drills that inject failures (null spikes, late partitions, DAG failures) to test alerts and runbooks end to end.
Lint in CI that every P1/P2 alert has a valid runbook link and that runbook commands reference existing DAGs/models.
Periodically test the escalation policy by simulating an unacknowledged page to confirm it cascades to the secondary and lead.

commonMistakes.mistake: Paging only on infrastructure health and job success, not on data freshness and quality.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Teams reuse generic web-SRE alerting that watches CPU, memory, and job exit codes and assume a green DAG means good data.
commonMistakes.impact: Stale or wrong data reaches dashboards and ML features undetected, and the incident is discovered hours later by a stakeholder.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Add freshness, volume, and quality (dbt test / Great Expectations) alerts wired to the pager so data problems page even when infrastructure is healthy.

commonMistakes.mistake: Alerting on everything, so every alert pages a human.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: It feels safer to page on any anomaly, and severity is not defined per alert.
commonMistakes.impact: Alert fatigue sets in, engineers ignore or auto-dismiss pages, and genuine P1s are missed while burnout rises.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Assign severities (P1-P4), page only on actionable business-impacting events, and route the rest to Slack, tickets, or dashboards; regularly prune noisy alerts.

commonMistakes.mistake: Alerts with no runbook, or stale runbooks that no longer match the pipeline.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Runbooks are written once and never maintained, or treated as optional documentation to do later.
commonMistakes.impact: On-call engineers cannot resolve incidents without the original author, so MTTR balloons and escalations spike at 3 AM.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Require a runbook link on every actionable alert, keep runbooks in version control next to the pipeline, and update them in the same PR that changes the pipeline.

commonMistakes.mistake: Blindly retrying or backfilling without checking root cause or idempotency.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Re-running is the fastest way to make a red DAG green, and pressure is high during an incident.
commonMistakes.impact: Non-idempotent reruns duplicate data, wide backfills waste compute, and retrying a non-transient failure just hides the real bug.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Diagnose first, ensure loads are idempotent (MERGE/delete-insert), scope backfills to the affected partition, and only auto-retry failures known to be transient.

comparisonSection.explanation: Web SRE pages mostly on availability and latency of a running service. Data on-call also pages on freshness breaches, volume drops, and failed quality tests, because a data product can be technically 'up' and running while delivering stale or wrong data.

Actionable, business-impacting events (P1/P2) should page a human 24/7 or during coverage hours. Non-actionable or low-priority signals (P3/P4) should go to Slack, tickets, or dashboards; paging on FYI events is the main cause of alert fatigue.

Manual triage gives full control but costs engineer time and sleep for repetitive, well-understood failures. Auto-remediation (Airflow retries, automatic partition backfills, quarantine) resolves known transient issues without paging, cutting toil and MTTR, but must be reserved for failures known to be safe to retry.

A single rotation is simple but concentrates night pages on one region and risks burnout. Follow-the-sun passes the pager between regions so on-call happens in local daytime, reducing night pages, but requires a distributed team and disciplined handoffs.

beginnerQuestions.question: What does on-call mean for a data engineering team?
beginnerQuestions.answer: It means a designated engineer is responsible for responding to production data incidents during a defined window, including pipeline failures, freshness SLA breaches, and data quality violations, using runbooks and an escalation policy to resolve them quickly.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: A strong answer stresses that data on-call pages on data problems (freshness, quality), not just infrastructure, and mentions rotations and runbooks.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is a runbook and what should it contain?
beginnerQuestions.answer: A runbook is a per-alert document that tells the on-call engineer how to respond. It should contain the symptom, the business impact/blast radius, the severity, ordered diagnosis steps, safe mitigation actions (retry, backfill, rollback), the escalation path, and links to dashboards and lineage.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Interviewers want the concrete anatomy of a runbook, not just 'documentation for incidents'.

beginnerQuestions.question: What do MTTA and MTTR mean?
beginnerQuestions.answer: MTTA is Mean Time To Acknowledge, the average time from an alert firing to a human acknowledging it. MTTR is Mean Time To Resolve/Recover, the average time from alert to full resolution. Together they measure response speed and total data downtime.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: The interviewer checks you know both metrics and that MTTR is the key downtime target while MTTA reflects notification/rotation health.

intermediateQuestions.question: How would you set up alerting so it pages on data problems, not just job failures?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Wire multiple signal sources into the pager: an Airflow on_failure_callback for DAG/task failures, scheduled freshness checks on key tables, and dbt tests or Great Expectations checkpoints for quality. Each alert carries a severity, dedup key, and runbook link, and routes P1/P2 to PagerDuty while P3/P4 go to Slack or tickets.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: A good answer connects concrete tools (Airflow, dbt, Great Expectations) to severity-tiered routing and runbooks.

intermediateQuestions.question: How do you reduce alert fatigue on a data team?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Assign proper severities and page only on actionable, business-impacting events; route FYI to Slack/tickets; dedup and group related alerts; make alerts self-resolve when checks pass; auto-remediate transient failures before paging; and regularly review on-call metrics to prune noisy or always-firing alerts.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Interviewers want a systematic approach: severity, dedup, auto-resolve, auto-remediation, and metric-driven pruning.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is the difference between a primary/secondary rotation and an escalation policy?
intermediateQuestions.answer: The rotation schedule assigns who is on duty (primary first responder, secondary backup) for each window. The escalation policy defines what happens over time if an alert is not acknowledged or resolved, cascading from primary to secondary to lead to manager. The rotation is 'who', the escalation policy is 'when it cascades and to whom'.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Distinguishing schedule (who is on duty) from escalation (how unacked incidents cascade) shows real operational understanding.

advancedQuestions.question: How would you design auto-remediation for common data pipeline failures?
advancedQuestions.answer: Classify failures into transient (network blips, brief upstream lateness) and non-transient (schema change, bad data). For transient ones use Airflow retries with exponential backoff and automatic partition backfills once the upstream partition lands, all on idempotent loads so reruns are safe; quarantine bad rows for quality failures. Only page a human when auto-remediation fails or the failure is classified non-transient, and always record what was auto-fixed.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Strong answers emphasize failure classification, idempotency, and paging only on non-remediable failures, plus observability of auto-fixes.

advancedQuestions.question: How do you measure and improve on-call health for a data team?
advancedQuestions.answer: Track MTTA, MTTR, total pages per week, after-hours/night pages, percent of alerts auto-resolved, and escalation rate. Review them regularly to find noisy alerts to prune, recurring failures to auto-remediate, and unfair rotation load. Improvements include follow-the-sun rotations, better severity tiering, and investing in the top MTTR-driving runbooks.
advancedQuestions.explanation: The interviewer looks for concrete metrics and a feedback loop from metrics to alert tuning, auto-remediation, and rotation design.

advancedQuestions.question: How do you handle handoff and knowledge transfer between on-call shifts?
advancedQuestions.answer: Do a structured handoff at rotation end covering open incidents and their state, known-flaky pipelines, in-flight backfills, and any suppressed alerts. Capture this in a shared handoff doc or channel, keep runbooks current, and hold blameless postmortems for significant incidents so learnings are shared across future responders.
advancedQuestions.explanation: A good answer treats handoff as a defined process (open incidents, flaky pipelines, in-flight backfills) plus postmortems, not an informal chat.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: At 05:50 UTC you are paged: the revenue dashboard's source table has not refreshed and the 06:30 executive deadline is at risk. How do you respond?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: This is a freshness breach on a revenue-critical (P1) table with a hard deadline. First acknowledge to stop MTTA and signal ownership, then open the runbook and quickly determine root cause: DAG/task failure vs upstream lateness vs quality test failure. Check blast radius in lineage and communicate to stakeholders early given the deadline.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Acknowledge the page, open the linked runbook, and run its diagnosis: 'airflow tasks states-for-dag-run' to see the failed task, parse dbt run_results.json for a failing model/test, and query source freshness in Snowflake to check for upstream lateness. If a null spike broke a not_null test, quarantine the bad rows and run 'dbt build --select stg_orders+'; if the upstream partition was late, run an idempotent partition-scoped backfill. Post an early status in #data-incidents given the deadline, escalate to the ingestion secondary if the root cause is upstream, verify the freshness SLA is restored, and file a postmortem plus an auto-remediation follow-up since it is a recurring failure mode.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: Your team is getting paged 40 times a week and engineers are burning out and missing real incidents. What do you do?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: 40 pages a week signals severe alert fatigue and probably many non-actionable pages. I need data on where pages come from and which are actionable, then aggressively tier, dedup, auto-resolve, and auto-remediate, and finally review rotation load.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Pull PagerDuty analytics to rank alerts by volume and by percent that were actionable. Downgrade non-actionable alerts from paging to Slack/tickets, add dedup keys to collapse storms, make alerts self-resolve when checks pass, and add Airflow retries plus automatic backfills so transient failures never page. Reserve P1/P2 for business-impacting events with runbooks. Track total pages and after-hours pages weekly and set a target, and rebalance the rotation (or move to follow-the-sun) to spread load. The goal is fewer, higher-signal pages so real P1s are never missed.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design an on-call and alerting system for a data platform with hundreds of pipelines feeding critical dashboards and ML features.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Emit signals from Airflow callbacks, scheduled freshness checks, and dbt/Great Expectations tests, each tagged with severity, a dedup key, and a runbook link. Route them to PagerDuty/Opsgenie which resolves the primary from a weekly rotation and cascades via an escalation policy to secondary and leads. Store runbooks in version control next to pipelines, expose freshness and on-call health metrics in Grafana, and add auto-remediation (retries, backfills, quarantine) for known transient failures.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: More alerts improve coverage but risk alert fatigue, so severity tiering and auto-resolve are essential. Auto-remediation cuts toil but can hide real bugs if applied to non-transient failures. 24/7 coverage improves reliability but strains small teams, favoring follow-the-sun or business-hours tiers.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Tier alerts and runbooks by data value, dedup and group alerts to prevent storms, push routine recovery into auto-remediation so operational load stays flat, centralize ownership metadata and lineage for fast blast-radius assessment, and continuously prune noisy alerts using on-call health metrics.

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: Data on-call is the practice of a designated engineer, backed by rotations, escalation policies, severity-tiered alerts, and runbooks, responding to data incidents (pipeline failures, freshness breaches, quality violations) to minimize data downtime.
keyConcepts: Data on-call pages on freshness/volume/quality, not just infrastructure or job success.
Rotation = who is on duty (primary/secondary); escalation policy = how unacked pages cascade.
Severity P1-P4: only actionable, business-impacting events should page a human.
Every actionable alert needs a runbook: symptom, impact, diagnosis, mitigation, escalation, links.
Auto-remediate known transient failures (retry, backfill, quarantine) on idempotent loads.
formulas: MTTA = total acknowledge time / number of incidents
MTTR = total resolution time / number of incidents
Page load = pages per engineer per rotation week
commands: dbt rebuild + downstream: dbt build --select stg_orders+
dbt test a model: dbt test --select stg_orders
Inspect dbt results: jq '.results[] | select(.status!="pass")' target/run_results.json
interviewPoints: Data on-call pages on data problems, not only service downtime.
Distinguish rotation (who) from escalation policy (when it cascades).
Reserve paging for actionable P1/P2; route FYI to Slack/tickets.
A runbook is part of the alert, not optional documentation.
Idempotent loads make retries and backfills safe; classify failures before auto-retrying.
quickNotes: A green DAG is not the same as fresh, correct data.
Track MTTA, MTTR, page volume, and after-hours pages.
Dedup keys and self-resolving alerts cut pager noise.
Follow-the-sun reduces night pages and burnout.
Do a structured handoff: open incidents, flaky pipelines, in-flight backfills.

keyTakeaways: On-call for data teams means a designated engineer responds to pipeline failures, freshness breaches, and quality violations, not just infrastructure outages, because a green pipeline can still deliver stale or wrong data.
Rotations (primary/secondary, optionally follow-the-sun) plus an escalation policy guarantee a clear owner and ensure unacknowledged incidents reliably cascade to someone with more context.

Severity tiering (P1-P4) with paging reserved for actionable, business-impacting events, combined with dedup and self-resolving alerts, is the key to controlling pager noise and avoiding alert fatigue.

Every actionable alert must link to a version-controlled runbook containing symptom, impact, diagnosis steps, mitigation, escalation, and links to dashboards and lineage, so any engineer can resolve it quickly.
Reducing MTTA and MTTR relies on auto-remediation of common failures (retries, idempotent backfills, quarantine), structured handoffs, and continuous review of on-call health metrics.
